ties.name: Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace
ties.plain: Nonexistence of global smooth bounded-energy flow on ℝ³

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal statement defines the following assertion; a proof requires a separate theorem. For each viscosity $
u>0$ there is a smooth, compactly supported field $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}u_0=0$ for which no pair $u:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$, $p:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ has all of the following properties: joint smoothness up to $t=0$ on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$; $u(0)=u_0$; $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u=
u\Delta u-
abla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ for every $t>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$; and one finite constant $A$ with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx\le A$ for every $t\ge0$. The single bound is uniform over the entire half-line, not a separate bound on each finite interval. The integral is the nonnegative integral, so an infinite energy cannot satisfy the inequality. A real upper bound is converted to its nonnegative part, which does not alter existence of a finite bound. Functions are defined also for negative times, but no condition is imposed there. This statement gives no blow-up time, trajectory, rate, or profile-comparison estimate.

The formal statement specifies the whole-space failure of a global smooth solution with one uniform energy bound; it does not formulate the historical regularity problem or a finite blow-up trajectory.
rows.name: Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace
rows.plain: Nonexistence of global smooth bounded-energy flow on ℝ³
rows.annotation: The datum is chosen before the negation of global existence: for each $\nu>0$ there is one smooth compactly supported solenoidal $u_0$ for which no global smooth pair $(u,p)$ has $\sup_{t\ge0}\|u(t)\|_2^2<\infty$. In particular the claim concerns all global solutions from that datum.

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal statement defines the following assertion; a proof requires a separate theorem. For each viscosity $
u>0$ there is a smooth field $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0(x+e_i)=u_0(x)$ for each coordinate vector $e_i$ and $\operatorname{div}u_0=0$, such that no pair of globally defined functions $u(t,x),p(t,x)$ is jointly smooth on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$, has $u(0)=u_0$, satisfies $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u=
u\Delta u-
abla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ for every $t>0$, and has $u(t,x+e_i)=u(t,x)$ for every $t\ge0$. These periodic fields represent fields on $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. Periodicity is required of the velocity only. The excluded pressure may be any smooth scalar field on $\mathbb R^3$, including a nonperiodic one. There is no separate energy condition, prescribed mean, blow-up time, two-sided rate, or comparison on a ball. Values at negative times have no role.

The formal statement specifies the periodic failure of a global smooth velocity and leaves pressure periodicity unrestricted.
rows.name: Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus
rows.plain: Nonexistence of global smooth flow on the unit torus
rows.annotation: For periodic velocity the energy over a period cell is automatically finite at each time. The formal target imposes no uniform energy bound on the half-line and allows nonperiodic pressure. The moving-frame reduction in the proof removes the linear-in-space part of the pressure without changing the initial datum.

ties.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
ties.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators, with $C$ compact. Let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ and $\|T_0\|\le b$, and write $T=T_0+C$. This assertion says that there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$, and a bounded projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$, whose range is finite-dimensional, such that $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$ for every natural number $n$ and every $x\in\mathcal X$. The restriction of $T$ maps the range of $P_u$ onto itself. Hence the complement has a controlled forward evolution and the finite-dimensional part has a controlled inverse evolution. The inequalities imply $r_2>0$, so the reciprocal in $r_2^{-n}$ is an ordinary reciprocal. The formulation uses projections and powers rather than a list of complex eigenvalues. It does not impose the existence or size of an unstable eigenvalue. Taking $b=\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$ is the application to the period map.

The formal assertion provides a finite-dimensional commuting projection for every compact perturbation of a small bounded operator, without assuming a particular unstable eigenvalue; it is the spectral input rather than the nonlinear stability conclusion.
rows.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
rows.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation
rows.annotation: The spectral circle $|z|=\Theta$ lies strictly inside the unit circle. Thus a mode with $\Theta<|z|<1$ must also be accounted for, although its amplitude tends to zero. The number of conditions on the datum is the dimension of the exterior spectral subspace, including generalized eigenvectors.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.

The correction component of the linear right inverse lies in a fixed finite-dimensional space; nonlinear stability and the physical norm identification require the subsequent contraction and realization.
rows.name: Breakdown.StepDataStatement
rows.plain: Interval splitting and right-inverse data for the linearized equation
rows.annotation: The finite-dimensional conditions are on a spectral projection of the datum. We may realize any prescribed value of this projection by a compactly supported solenoidal field (proof of Proposition 4.3). This is what permits the correction of a cutoff datum even when the exceptional spectral vectors themselves have no known spatial decay.

ties.name: Breakdown.certificate_orbit
ties.plain: A rectangular-parameter certificate gives a recurrent weak profile

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem takes the earlier rectangular-box certificate as a premise and concludes existence of a recurrent weak profile; its conclusion does not state smoothness, closeness, or the prescribed symmetry group of the current paper.
rows.name: Breakdown.certificate_orbit
rows.plain: A rectangular-parameter certificate gives a recurrent weak profile
rows.annotation: A small residual measures how nearly the approximate field solves the equation, not how near it is to any solution. Section 7 supplies the missing inverse estimate, then controls the quadratic error and selects a member of the family for which the auxiliary force can be removed. The linked theorem assumes a certificate with a rectangular parameter set and constructs a weak recurrent profile; the inequalities for the concrete numerical data are a separate task.

ties.name: Breakdown.physicalTime
ties.plain: Logarithmic similarity time at final time one

rows.fidelity_note:
For a real phase $s_0$ and time $t<1$, this defines $s=s_0-\log(1-t)$. At $s_0=0$ it equals $\log(1/(1-t))$, the similarity time in (1.4) with $T=1$. No equation or profile hypothesis is included. The function is defined for all real $t$: the real logarithm is assigned the value zero at zero and uses the absolute value for a negative argument. These extensions carry no assertion about a solution at or after time one; all physical change-of-variable statements restrict to $t<1$, where $1-t>0$. For a general final time $T>0$, the paper instead uses $\log(T/(T-t))$.

The formal time variable is $s_0-\log(1-t)$; at $T=1,s_0=0$ it agrees with the paper.
rows.name: Breakdown.physicalTime
rows.plain: Logarithmic similarity time at final time one
rows.annotation: If $s=-\log(1-t)$, the physical times corresponding to $s$ and $s+S$ are $1-e^{-s}$ and $1-e^{-s-S}$. Their difference is $(1-t)(1-e^{-S})$. The fixed interval of similarity time therefore gives a sequence of shrinking physical intervals, which accumulate only at time one.

rows.fidelity_note:
For $t<1$, the scale is $a(t)=\sqrt{(1-t)^{-1}}=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. Multiplying $x\in\mathbb R^3$ by $a(t)$ gives the similarity position. The function is defined for every real $t$; division by zero is assigned zero, and the real square root of a nonpositive number is zero. Consequently its value is zero at and after $t=1$. These values serve only to define a function everywhere. They do not extend the physical solution through its final time. The paper's general scale is $(T-t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<T$.

The formal spatial scale is $(1-t)^{-1/2}$ on $t<1$; the paper allows any $T>0$.
rows.name: Breakdown.physicalScale
rows.plain: Similarity space scale (1 − t)⁻¹⁄²
rows.annotation: The velocity scale and the reciprocal spatial length scale are both $a(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. In `physicalScale` this is the factor applied to both $W$ and its spatial argument. The corresponding dilation parameter in (3.4) is $a(t)^2$, not $a(t)$.

ties.name: Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists
ties.plain: Nonzero smooth profile recurrent up to an orthogonal map

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be jointly smooth. For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, assume $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume one real constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integers $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in all $s,y$. Here $D_y^0W=W$, while for $j=1,2$ the derivative is a linear or bilinear map with its operator norm. The paper uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. These norms are equivalent in dimension three, with fixed factors; an unspecified bound transfers after enlarging $C$, but the same numerical constant is not asserted. In addition, there are $S>0$ and an orthogonal linear map $R:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ such that $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ for every $s,y$, and $W(s,y)
e0$ for at least one pair $(s,y)$. Both rotations and orientation-reversing orthogonal maps are admitted. No recurrence condition is imposed on $q$ itself. This is the assertion that some such $W,q,S,R,C$ exist. It supplies no numerical example and no chosen period or rotation. The profile used as a premise is more restrictive than the pair of decay inequalities printed in (1.3): second derivatives and the pressure gradient are also bounded. The denominator is always positive. The pressure is determined only to the extent imposed by its equation and gradient bound; time-dependent spatial constants are not fixed.

The formal existence assertion quantifies over some positive period and some orthogonal map; the paper fixes $S,R$ and then defines a profile with those values.
rows.name: Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists
rows.plain: Nonzero smooth profile recurrent up to an orthogonal map
rows.annotation: The return fixes a time interval $S$, not necessarily a least period. Iteration gives $W(s+nS,y)=R^nW(s,R^{-n}y)$. In particular the $L^p$ and gradient norms on balls about the origin is periodic in $s$, although the velocity at a fixed point need not be. Even when $R^2$ is a rotation, it need not be the identity.

ties.name: Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists
ties.plain: Nonzero smooth profile recurrent up to an orthogonal map

rows.fidelity_note: The formal premise uses jointly smooth functions on all real similarity times and on Euclidean three-space and requires $W(s,y)\ne0$ somewhere; the decay and recurrence clauses are separate components of that premise.
rows.name: Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists
rows.plain: Nonzero smooth profile recurrent up to an orthogonal map
rows.annotation: Only the velocity must be nonzero somewhere, and only the velocity is required to recur. The equations do imply $\nabla q(s+S,y)=R\nabla q(s,R^{-1}y)$; thus a pressure normalized by $q(s,0)=0$ would have the corresponding return law. No such choice of gauge is needed in `PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists`.

ties.plain: The similarity momentum residual

assessments.fidelity_note: The formal expression is the left-hand side of the momentum equation; its definition alone asserts neither that it vanishes nor that $W$ is divergence-free.

rows.name: Breakdown.SimilarityResidual
rows.plain: The similarity momentum residual
rows.annotation: With $\delta=T-t$, the identities $ds/dt=\delta^{-1}$ and $\partial_t y=y/(2\delta)$ give $\partial_t u=\delta^{-3/2}(\partial_sW+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2)$. The diffusion, advection and pressure gradient have the same factor $\delta^{-3/2}$. Dividing it out gives `SimilarityResidual`, including the positive signs of the two drift terms.

assessments.fidelity_note: The full display (1.2) consists of the similarity momentum equation, $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$. This formal condition imposes the first two identities for every $(s,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and assumes joint smoothness, decay through two spatial derivatives, and $|\nabla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. It contains neither $S$ nor $R$, so it cannot assert the third identity. The component comparison with the first line alone can be exact; the comparison with the entire numbered display is different.
The vanishing-residual and divergence components impose these equations pointwise for every $(s,y)$; the containing condition has further smoothness and decay requirements.

rows.fidelity_note: The full display (1.2) consists of the similarity momentum equation, $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$. This formal condition imposes the first two identities for every $(s,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and assumes joint smoothness, decay through two spatial derivatives, and $|\nabla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. It contains neither $S$ nor $R$, so it cannot assert the third identity. The component comparison with the first line alone can be exact; the comparison with the entire numbered display is different.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile
rows.plain: Smooth decaying similarity profile recurrent up to an orthogonal map
rows.annotation: `IsSimilarityProfile` is the local equation-and-decay part of the profile hypothesis; neither recurrence nor nonvanishing is included. One constant $C$ controls the velocity and its first two spatial derivatives, with one more inverse power of $1+|y|$ at each differentiation, as well as $\nabla q$. The last bound is additional to (1.3) and Remark 1.2.

assessments.fidelity_note: The formal existence assertion includes all three identities of (1.2) for every real $s$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, with some $S>0$ and $R\in O(3)$. It additionally requires smooth $W,q$, nonzero $W$, velocity decay through order two, and pressure-gradient decay. ties.name: Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn

rows.fidelity_note:

The integral is the extended nonnegative integral of the squared Euclidean norm. In the formula, a real bound $A$ is replaced by $\max(A,0)$; the existential condition is therefore equivalent to the existence of a finite nonnegative bound. rows.name: Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus
rows.plain: Nonexistence of global smooth flow on the unit torus
rows.annotation: Periodicity of $u$ implies periodicity of $\nabla p$ by the momentum equation. Thus $p(t,x+e_j)-p(t,x)=b_j(t)$ is independent of $x$. Choose $a''=-b$, $a(0)=a'(0)=0$. Then $u(t,x+a(t))-a'(t)$ solves the equation with pressure $p(t,x+a(t))+a''(t)\cdot x$, up to an additive function of time. The pressure increments are $b_j+a_j''=0$ and the initial velocity is unchanged.

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal statement defines an existence assertion on the unit torus. There are a smooth field $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with period one in each coordinate and zero divergence, a real $T>0$, and a continuous mild curve $u$ on $[0,T)$ whose initial state is the Fourier representation of $u_0$, such that $\sup_{0\le t<T}\|u(t)\|=\infty$. The periodic state has coordinates $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,\widehat u(k)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$, with conjugate symmetry and $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$; its norm is the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm on the unit cell. The zero coefficient is allowed, so this state space does not impose zero mean. The initial-field map returns zero outside its admissible Fourier class; smooth periodic solenoidal data belong to that class. Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation for every $0\le t<T$, with convergent time integrals. The assertion imposes neither $T\le1$ nor either estimate in (1.7), gives no local comparison on $B_{1/16}$, and states unboundedness rather than a specified limit or rate at $T$. It contains no smooth velocity-pressure representative of the curve. The formal statement is only this existence condition; a separate construction proves it from a profile.

The formal condition gives a periodic mild curve on $[0,T)$ with some $T>0$ and unbounded inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; it does not state $T\le1$, smoothness, the rate, or the local comparison.

Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+P)=\rho w(s)$ with $P>0$. Put $S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

The formal statement proves that there exists $c>0$ with $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$. In the whole-space realization the norm is $\dot H^1$, and dilation gives $\|u^*(t)\|\ge c(1-t)^{-1/4}$ for $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$ and $0\le t<1$. The formal conclusion is the lower bound on the recurrent orbit; it does not include a nearby solution $u$, the upper bound in (2.5), the chosen constant $c_*/2$, or uniformity over all nearby data $w_0$. Those require the quantitative correction and a separate upper bound for the orbit.

For a nonzero recurrent mild orbit in the stated Hilbert setting, the formal result gives one positive lower norm bound for every real similarity time.
rows.name: Breakdown.orbitNorm
rows.plain: A recurrent mild orbit has a uniform positive norm lower bound
rows.annotation: The norm of a recurrent slice is a continuous periodic function of $s$. If it vanished at some phase, the mild solution starting at that phase would have zero datum and would remain zero; recurrence would then make all earlier slices zero as well. Hence the minimum on a period is positive. `orbitNorm` obtains a stronger conclusion by excluding all slices below a positive small-data threshold for the mild theory.

rows.annotation: Put $\chi=w_0-W(0)$ and let $J_0$ be the inverse of $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$. rows.plain: Nearby dense initial data give mild flow tracking the recurrent profile
rows.annotation: The quantifiers differ. `TransferHolds` is enough to find one datum in any prescribed dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$, arbitrarily close to $W(0)$. abla q=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume one real constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integers $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in all $s,y$. Here $D_y^0W=W$, while for $j=1,2$ the derivative is a linear or bilinear map with its operator norm. The paper uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. These norms are equivalent in dimension three, with fixed factors; an unspecified bound transfers after enlarging $C$, but the same numerical constant is not asserted. This condition does not require a positive period, an orthogonal recurrence, or nonzero velocity. Those are separate assumptions in the existence statement. In particular, this condition by itself includes the zero field. All denominators are positive because $1+|y|>0$. The derivative bounds are for the three natural-number orders $0,1,2$, rather than for every real order. The pressure-gradient bound and the second-derivative bound are additional explicit assumptions compared with (1.2) and (1.3).

The formal condition assumes decay through two spatial derivatives and pressure-gradient decay. It does not prove this implication from velocity decay alone, and its derivative bounds use operator norms.

rows.annotation: Let $\delta=T-t$ and $r=\tfrac12\max(|x|,\sqrt\delta)$. On the backward cylinder of radius $r$, either $|x'|\ge|x|/2$ or $T-t'\ge\delta$, according to which scale defines $r$. Hence $r|u^*|\lesssim C_W$ on that cylinder. Rescaling the interior derivative estimate back gives $|\nabla_x^j u^*(t,x)|\lesssim r^{-1-j}$ for $j=1,2$; converting to $y$ gives the two velocity derivative bounds. `IsSimilarityProfile` also assumes the pressure-gradient estimate, which is not supplied by this remark.

rows.name: Breakdown.certificate_orbit
rows.plain: A rectangular-parameter certificate gives a recurrent weak profile
rows.annotation: In Sections 4–6 the reference profile is already an exact solution, and the unknown correction changes the initial datum so that the new solution follows it toward blow-up. Here the problem is to construct that reference profile in the first place: the correction changes a periodic field and the parameter selects its period. The two corrections have different purposes; neither requires the reference velocity itself to have finite kinetic energy.

rows.name: Breakdown.certificate_orbit
rows.plain: A rectangular-parameter certificate gives a recurrent weak profile
rows.annotation: There is one parameter for each forcing coefficient, and the period is a given function $S(\alpha)$ of these parameters. At fixed $\alpha$ the correction problem has unknowns $(v,\beta)$; the approximate velocity and its coefficients $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ are given. The remaining task is to find $\alpha$ with $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta=0$. The linked Lean theorem uses the earlier rectangular parameter set rather than the more general set (7.29).

rows.name: Breakdown.certificate_orbit
rows.plain: A rectangular-parameter certificate gives a recurrent weak profile
rows.annotation: In the inverse estimate (7.18) it is the given coefficient field that is represented by finitely many numbers. The unknown $v$ ranges over the whole class $\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}^\Gamma$, with no truncation in space or frequency and no smallness condition. Appendix B must control the components not represented in the finite cell inequalities as well as the represented ones. Only when a small residual is inserted into this uniform estimate can one infer the smallness of a correction.

At this parameter the change of force coefficients is $\beta=-\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$, which is why the squared norm of $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ appears beside the squared correction norm. rows.annotation: There are two kinds of numerical input. For a given field, such as $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, one can enclose its norms and pairings directly. For the linear estimate one must instead establish a quadratic inequality for arbitrary perturbations. In Appendix B the finite matrix tests are accompanied by estimates for omitted polynomial coefficients, harmonics and the spatial exterior. Their purpose is to give the estimate on the whole domain, not just on the space used to compute the approximate solution.

rows.annotation: The perturbation is required to have the same space-time symmetries as the approximate field. Consequently the linearized and quadratic terms stay in that class, and the inverse estimate need only hold there. For instance, a rotation after half a period gives a half-period for the gradient energy, even when the velocity itself needs the full period; this improves (7.55).

rows.annotation: There is no residual when the uncut $u^*$ is substituted in the whole-space equation. Its momentum equation follows from the local rescaling calculation, not from recurrence. Recurrence enters when solving for the perturbation through successive shrinking intervals. The linked result proves the rescaled classical equations before the final time.

rows.name: Breakdown.TransferHolds
rows.plain: Nearby dense initial data give mild flow tracking the recurrent profile
rows.annotation: Only the reference is recurrent. For its perturbation, the return map is a compact perturbation of a map of norm at most $e^{-S/4}$. The desired rate $e^{-\kappa S}$ is chosen strictly above this bound and off the spectrum. The initial correction prescribes the exterior projection for that rate; it does not require spectral stability.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay
ties.plain: L⁶ Sobolev bound for smooth decaying solenoidal fields

rows.fidelity_note: The authors’ proved inequality for smooth decaying fields controls the L6 velocity by the square-integrable gradient. The radial powers here are obtained from the paper’s (1.3).
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay
rows.plain: L⁶ Sobolev bound for smooth decaying solenoidal fields
rows.annotation: For $R\ge1$, (1.3) gives $\int_{|y|>R}|W|^6\lesssim C_W^6 R^{-3}$ and $\int_{|y|>R}|\nabla W|^2\lesssim C_W^2 R^{-1}$, uniformly in $s$. Together with the bounds on the unit ball this puts each slice in $X$. The velocity bound $O(|y|^{-1})$ does not alone imply $L^2$ integrability, which is why the whole-space construction in §5 cuts off the datum.

ties.name: Breakdown.MildRegular
ties.plain: Smooth representatives of a mild curve

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the following regularity property of a realization of $X$ and a bounded linear map $V:X\to L^6$. Let $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\rm div}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $T_0>0$, and let $u$ be a continuous mild curve in the supplied real Hilbert space $X$ on the closed interval $[0,T_0]$, with $u(0)$ equal to the supplied realization of $\varphi$. Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation, with each time integral convergent. The regularity conclusion gives fields $U,P$ jointly smooth up to the boundary of $[0,T_0]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $U(0)=\varphi$, $\operatorname{div}U=0$ throughout that closed interval and $\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U=\Delta U-\nabla P$ for $0<t<T_0$. Each $U(t)$ equals $V(u(t))\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, for the supplied bounded linear map $V:X\to L^6$ almost everywhere. There are finite constants $A,B$ such that $\int|U(t)|^2\le A$ and $|U(t,x)|,\|D_xU(t,x)\|_{\rm op}\le B$ for all $t\in[0,T_0]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$. This whole-space property is proved for the frequency realization of $\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ used in the paper; it does not contain the periodic assertion in the quoted sentence.
rows.name: Breakdown.MildRegular
rows.plain: Smooth representatives of a mild curve
rows.annotation: For each $b<T$ the mild curve is bounded in the gradient norm on $[0,b]$. A smooth compactly supported datum also lies in inhomogeneous $H^1$, so the local solution in that space can be identified with the mild curve by uniqueness. `MildRegular` is the closed-interval whole-space formulation of the resulting regularity property; it additionally requires bounded energy and a bounded velocity and gradient. It is proved by `mildRegular_realization`, not by the definition itself.

ties.name: Breakdown.Periodic.V
ties.plain: The periodic Fourier space

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The conjugate symmetry is the reality condition and $n\cdot a(n)=0$ is the divergence-free condition. At $n=0$ the latter gives no restriction, which is why nonzero constants are included. The space is a closed real subspace of $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and is complete. A nonzero constant has positive formal norm and zero gradient norm, so the mean-zero restriction is essential in (3.16). Equation (3.15) instead uses the homogeneous norm on mean-zero fields of arbitrary period $L$. The distinction matters: the zero Fourier mode contributes to the formal norm, and no variable spatial period is a parameter of an element of the formal space.

The formal unit-torus space uses the inhomogeneous $H^1$ weight $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$ and retains the zero Fourier coefficient; mean zero is not part of that space definition.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.V
rows.plain: The periodic Fourier space
rows.annotation: The mean-zero condition removes the constants, on which the gradient norm vanishes. On a cell of side $L$, Poincaré gives $\|u\|_2\le (L/2\pi)\|\nabla u\|_2$, but the Sobolev bound $\|u\|_6\lesssim\|\nabla u\|_2$ has a constant independent of $L$. The latter bound is needed for the contraction on large tori. In `V` the period is already one; the full $H^1$ norm is used and constants are allowed.

ties.name: Breakdown.SimilarityResidual
ties.plain: The similarity momentum residual

rows.fidelity_note:
For functions $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$, the value at $(s,y)$ is $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q$. This defines a vector-valued expression. It does not assert that the expression is zero, that $W$ is divergence-free, or that $W$ is recurrent. Nor does the definition itself assume differentiability: derivative operations have assigned values where a classical derivative does not exist. In every smooth-profile application the smoothness hypotheses ensure that all terms are the ordinary derivatives appearing in (1.2). The spatial Laplacian is the sum of the pure second derivatives, and the spatial derivative of $W$ applied to $y$ is $(y\cdot
abla)W$.

The formal expression records the similarity momentum equation, but the definition alone does not prove equivalence under the change of variables.
rows.name: Breakdown.SimilarityResidual
rows.plain: The similarity momentum residual
rows.annotation:
On substituting $U=W+V$ in (1.2), the terms containing only $W$ vanish. The linearized convection is $(W\cdot
abla)V+(V\cdot
abla)W$, and the only remaining quadratic term is $(V\cdot
abla)V$. The equations for $V$ have the free drift and diffusion of (1.2), but no prescribed return law. One seeks decay of $V$, not a second periodic orbit.

rows.fidelity_note:
For any $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and real phase $s_0$, the field at $t<1$ is $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. Thus it agrees with (1.4) for $T=1$ and $s_0=0$. It is a definition of the change of variables, with no smoothness, equation, or recurrence hypothesis. With a general $T>0$ the paper's field satisfies $u_T^*(t,x)=T^{-1/2}u_1^*(t/T,x/\sqrt T)$ when the phase is zero. The formal function is defined at every real time; division by zero and the square root of a nonpositive number are assigned zero, so the defined field is zero for $t\ge1$. No claim of a solution at those times follows. All uses of the change of variables in the evolution restrict to $t<1$.

The definition supplies the final-time-one transformation; classical differentiability and the equations are required for the equivalence.
rows.name: Breakdown.physicalField
rows.plain: The physical velocity
rows.annotation: The difference $v=u-u^*$ is in physical variables, whereas $U-W=D_{1-t}v$ is in similarity variables. Their gradient norms differ by the factor $(1-t)^{1/4}$. This is the weight that is needed to control a physical perturbation through many shrinking periods.

rows.fidelity_note: The authors’ proved DilationAlgebra gives exactly the quarter power for the homogeneous norm under the Navier–Stokes dilation. Applying (1.4) gives the displayed exponents in the manuscript.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds
rows.plain: Dilation scales the homogeneous Sobolev norm by μ¹⁄⁴
rows.annotation: Set $r=1-t$. The identity $\|D_{1/r}f\|_X=r^{-1/4}\|f\|_X$ changes the similarity error $O(e^{-\kappa s})=O(r^\kappa)$ to a physical gradient error $O(r^{\kappa-1/4})$. Although this latter error need not tend to zero, its ratio to the reference gradient is $O(r^\kappa)$ by the lower bound of Lemma 4.2.

ties.name: Breakdown.MonodromyStatement
ties.plain: Short-step inverses and the compact monodromy correction

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$ be a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau)$ be symmetric bounded bilinear maps, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0,\tau>0$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, where $C_K\ge0$. For $\mu>0$, assume strongly continuous dilations satisfying $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For every $f$ in a dense subset of $X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with these operators at all their defined real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For every $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to converge and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. Choose an integer $k\ge1$, put $\lambda=e^{-S/k}$ and $h=1-\lambda$. On $Y=C([0,h];X)$ define $u_n^*(r)=D_{(1-r)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-r))$ and $A_nv(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(u_n^*(r),v(r))\,dr$. Assume $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every $n\ge0$. The assertion gives invertibility of $I-A_n$ and $\|(I-A_n)^{-1}\|\le4/3$. Put $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, $Lv=D_\lambda v(h)$, and $M_n=L(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$. It gives $M_{n+k}=\rho M_n\rho^{-1}$, compactness of $\rho^{-1}M_{k-1}\cdots M_0-\rho^{-1}(D_\lambda G(h))^k$, and $\|\rho^{-1}(D_\lambda G(h))^k\|\le e^{-S/4}$. For $k=1$, $(I-A_0)^{-1}\Gamma\chi$ is the solution $h_\chi$ of (4.9) on $[0,t_1]$ and $\rho^{-1}M_0$ is exactly $\mathcal M$ of (4.10). For larger $k$ the product computes the same period map over $k$ shorter steps; the formal statement does not state that identity. The subdivision and the bound $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ are explicit hypotheses, where the paper solves (4.9) by Lemma 3.4.
rows.name: Breakdown.MonodromyStatement
rows.plain: Short-step inverses and the compact monodromy correction
rows.annotation: The endpoint $h_\chi(t_1)$ is a physical velocity perturbation at the smaller spatial scale of the next period. Applying $D_\lambda$, with $\lambda=e^{-S}$, restores the original scale, and $\rho_R^{-1}$ restores the original orientation. Thus the output of the period map is in the same coordinates as its input; its powers describe successive normalized returns.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds
ties.plain: Heat semigroup on the homogeneous solenoidal space

rows.fidelity_note:
On the real Hilbert space $X$ of $L^2$ classes $g$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere, let $G(t)$ be multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$. The formal statement proves $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$, and continuity of $t\mapsto G(t)g$ on $[0,\infty)$ for each $g\in X$. It also states self-adjointness, $\langle G(t)g,h\rangle=\langle g,G(t)h\rangle$, for all real $t$, and confirms the indicated Fourier multiplier. An element $g$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, so $\|g\|_X$ corresponds to $\|\nabla u\|_2$ and $G(t)$ represents the paper's heat flow. Continuity is strong continuity for each fixed input, including the endpoint $0$; no continuity in operator norm at $0$ is asserted. Negative parameters use the identity extension and are outside the forward semigroup law.

The formal heat result gives contraction at nonnegative physical times; the additional dilation norm law produces the factor $e^{-s/4}$.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds
rows.plain: Heat semigroup on the homogeneous solenoidal space
rows.annotation: Heat alone gives a contraction of norm one in the gradient space: its Fourier multiplier approaches one at frequencies approaching zero. The strict bound for the free return is obtained from rescaling the heat-evolved field. This leaves a nontrivial interval of admissible spectral radii below one.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency space, with $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ representing a velocity. For $\mu>0$, its dilation acts by $g(\xi)\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$, which represents $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. The formal statement proves $\|D_\mu g\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|g\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$ for $\mu,
u>0$, and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $\mu>0$ and $t\ge0$, where $G(t)$ is the heat multiplier. It also confirms the stated action on frequency classes. The exponent $1/4$ is a real exponent. Although the formal dilation family has values at all real parameters, it is assigned zero for $\mu\le0$ and none of these positive-parameter identities uses those values. These conclusions establish the three identities of (3.5) in the Fourier representation.

The dilation factor at $\mu=e^{-s}$ is $e^{-s/4}$; applying the heat contraction gives the stated bound for $s\ge0$.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds
rows.plain: Dilation scales the homogeneous Sobolev norm by μ¹⁄⁴
rows.annotation: For $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ the gradient gains a factor $\mu$ and the volume element loses a factor $\mu^{3/2}$. Thus the squared gradient norm gains $\mu^{1/2}$ and the norm gains $\mu^{1/4}$. Setting $\mu=e^{-s}$ gives the factor $e^{-s/4}$ in the free similarity evolution.

ties.name: Breakdown.dilateField
ties.plain: Navier–Stokes dilation of a field

rows.fidelity_note: The formal dilation is $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ for $\mu>0$.
rows.name: Breakdown.dilateField
rows.plain: Navier–Stokes dilation of a field
rows.annotation: The exponent $1/4$ is a consequence of the space dimension: the factor $\mu$ in $\nabla D_\mu f$ and the factor $\mu^{-3/2}$ in the volume element give $\mu^{1/2}$ for the squared gradient norm. `dilateField` defines this spatial action, while the norm identity is proved in `dilation_holds`.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal norm law is exactly the factor $\mu^{1/4}$ for positive dilation parameters.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds
rows.plain: Dilation scales the homogeneous Sobolev norm by μ¹⁄⁴
rows.annotation: For a dilation by $e^{-S}$ the norm factor is $e^{-S/4}$. In the free part of the return map the heat step is contractive and the orthogonal change of coordinates is isometric, so neither can increase this factor. The estimate is for the free operator; the linearized transport about the profile must still be treated separately in Section 4.

ties.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
ties.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation

rows.fidelity_note: The authors’ abstract dichotomy separates a decaying part by an exponential bound and gives a commuting finite-rank projection with a complementary reverse bound. The paper chooses the circle strictly inside the unit circle.
rows.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
rows.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation
rows.annotation: The adjective exterior refers to the radius $\Theta$, not to the unit circle. For example, a scalar multiplier $a$ with $\Theta<|a|<1$ decays in the usual norm but grows as $(|a|/\Theta)^n$ after division by the target decay rate. Its homogeneous contribution must be removed by the datum correction.

ties.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
ties.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators, with $C$ compact. Let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ and $\|T_0\|\le b$, and write $T=T_0+C$. This assertion says that there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$, and a bounded projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$, whose range is finite-dimensional, such that $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$ for every natural number $n$ and every $x\in\mathcal X$. The restriction of $T$ maps the range of $P_u$ onto itself. Hence the complement has a controlled forward evolution and the finite-dimensional part has a controlled inverse evolution. The inequalities imply $r_2>0$, so the reciprocal in $r_2^{-n}$ is an ordinary reciprocal. The formulation uses projections and powers rather than a list of complex eigenvalues. It does not impose the existence or size of an unstable eigenvalue. Taking $b=e^{-S/4}$ and choosing $\beta<1$ is the application to the period map.

The formal hypothesis requires only a compact perturbation of an operator with a norm bound; no prescribed unstable eigenvalue or spectral sign is assumed.
rows.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
rows.plain: Finite-dimensional spectral splitting of a compact perturbation
rows.annotation: An eigenvalue of modulus greater than one is neither assumed nor needed. If the exterior range is zero, the whole-space linear inverse can use $E=\{0\}$; otherwise $\dim E=\dim\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. The construction uses the existence of this finite-dimensional range without locating its spectrum.

ties.name: Breakdown.StepDataStatement
ties.plain: Interval splitting and right-inverse data for the linearized equation

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

The formal statement is this implication, and it is proved from the spectral dichotomy.

The formal construction chooses a per-subinterval weight $\theta$ with $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$ and controls a bounded sequence after dividing by $\theta^n$; relating it to $\Theta=\theta^k$ gives $\kappa\in(0,1/4)$.
rows.name: Breakdown.StepDataStatement
rows.plain: Interval splitting and right-inverse data for the linearized equation
rows.annotation: At $t_n=1-e^{-nS}$ the rescaled error norm is $e^{-nS/4}\|v(t_n)\|_X$. Condition (4.5) bounds it by $\Theta^n\|v\|_\kappa$, where $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$. In the subdivision into $k$ equal similarity-time steps, the corresponding weight is $\theta=\Theta^{1/k}$, so each complete period still costs a factor $\Theta$.

ties.name: Breakdown.discreteDichotomy
ties.plain: The unstable initial correction sums future forcing through inverse powers

rows.fidelity_note: The authors’ proof constructs the forced initial component by a convergent tail series in the projected subspace.
rows.name: Breakdown.discreteDichotomy
rows.note: The authors’ proof constructs the forced initial component by a convergent tail series in the projected subspace.
rows.plain: The unstable initial correction sums future forcing through inverse powers
rows.annotation: For the divided recurrence the source at index $n+j$ enters after $j+1$ returns. Its contribution to the required exterior value at $n$ is $-\Theta^j\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-j-1}P_{\mathrm u}c_{n+j}$, where $c_m=\Theta^{-m}f_m$. Thus the inverse-power exponent is $j+1$ while the power of the weight is only $j$. The formal `tailSum` includes $P_{\mathrm u}$ in its inverse operator $N$.

ties.name: Breakdown.exists_section
ties.plain: Lifting a finite-dimensional projection

rows.fidelity_note: The authors’ proof lifts a finite basis of the projected subspace through any dense subspace. The manuscript chooses compactly supported solenoidal test fields.
rows.name: Breakdown.exists_section
rows.note: The authors’ proof lifts a finite basis of the projected subspace through any dense subspace. The manuscript chooses compactly supported solenoidal test fields.
rows.plain: Lifting a finite-dimensional projection
rows.annotation: Fix a basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ and choose one compact solenoidal preimage for each basis vector. Their span is complementary to $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$, though it need not be invariant under the return map. The latter invariance is required only of the spectral subspaces used to evolve the recurrence.

ties.name: Breakdown.ContractionStatement
ties.plain: Small solution of the discrete quadratic correction equation

rows.fidelity_note: The formal contraction handles every small initial displacement in the abstract sequence problem. The finite-dimensional correction space and the identification with a continuous-time mild solution come from separate ingredients.
rows.name: Breakdown.ContractionStatement
rows.plain: Small solution of the discrete quadratic correction equation
rows.annotation: The nonlinear interaction is quadratic in the error, which becomes small in similarity variables. If the normalized error on short interval $n$ is $\theta^nz_n$, division of its equation by $\theta^n$ leaves the mixed operator unchanged and gives the quadratic term $\theta^n N(z_n,z_n)$. A single bound for $z$ in the supremum norm therefore suffices for the contraction on all intervals.

For $\mu>0$, assume strongly continuous dilations satisfying $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For every $f$ in a dense subset of $X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with these operators at all their defined real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. The application is $X=\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ and $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. Here mildness means $u(t)=G(t)u(0)+\int_0^tK(t-r)(u(r),u(r))\,dr$, with each Bochner integral convergent. The conclusion chooses one nearby datum. The paper's statement starts with each nearby prescribed datum and corrects it in a fixed finite-dimensional space; that stronger quantifier is not retained here.
rows.name: Breakdown.TransferHolds
rows.plain: Nearby dense initial data give mild flow tracking the recurrent profile
rows.annotation: For the application to compact data, it is enough that the initial datum be in the dense subspace of compact solenoidal fields and close to $W(0)$. The paper proves the stronger assertion that one fixed $E$ works for all nearby prescribed data, including ones outside that subspace. The linked formal conclusion does not state this uniform affine-space prescription.

rows.name: Breakdown.TransferHolds
rows.plain: Nearby dense initial data give mild flow tracking the recurrent profile
rows.annotation: For the recurrence $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$, impose $\chi_n=O(\Theta^n)$ with $\Theta$ strictly inside the exterior spectral radii. Multiplying the projected recurrence by the backward powers and summing gives $P_u\chi_0=-\sum_{m\ge0}M_u^{-(m+1)}P_uf_m$. The initial correction changes the projection of the given discrepancy to this value. The source itself depends on the nonlinear error, so the correction is determined together with the trajectory; neither the singular time nor the phase is varied.

ties.name: Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential
ties.plain: A vector potential along radial segments

rows.fidelity_note:
For a centre $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and field $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this defines $A(x)=\int_0^1 s\,g(x_0+s(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,ds$. The integral is a vector-valued Bochner integral over the scalar parameter $s$. For an arbitrary field the definition assigns zero to this integral when the integrand is not integrable. For smooth $g$ the integrand is continuous on the compact interval, so this is the ordinary integral. In the paper the centre is the origin; the formal formula permits any centre. This definition alone neither assumes $\operatorname{div}g=0$ nor proves $\operatorname{curl}A=g$. The latter identity requires the separate smoothness and divergence-free hypotheses. No decay at spatial infinity is needed to define this finite radial integral for smooth $g$.

At centre zero, the formal radial vector potential has the formula used for $A$; the statement also allows an arbitrary centre.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential
rows.plain: A vector potential along radial segments
rows.annotation: At fixed $t$, integrate the field along the segment from $0$ to $x$. The identity $\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x]=\partial_\sigma[\sigma^2 u^*(t,\sigma x)]$ follows from zero divergence. Thus the curl of the integral is determined by its two endpoints, giving $u^*(t,x)$. The formula `homotopyPotential` also allows the centre of the segments to be translated.

Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ and $\nabla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\rm op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $\chi$ be the fixed smooth cutoff with $0\le\chi\le1$, equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, set $\ell=T-t$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Define $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, $\bar u(x)=\chi(x)g(x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A_g(x)$, and $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell\,y)$. Thus $f$ is the cutoff expressed in similarity coordinates; its inner and outer radii are $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ and $1/(8\sqrt\ell)$. For every $T>0$, the formal statement proves that $(t,x)\mapsto\bar u(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$, is divergence-free, vanishes for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and equals $g$ for $|x-a|\le1/16$. rows.annotation: Periodization preserves the gradient norm of a field supported in one cell. It also preserves zero mean for a compact solenoidal $f$, since $f_j=\sum_m\partial_m(x_j f_m)$ and the integral of the derivative vanishes. ties.name: Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_holds
ties.plain: Fourth-power spatial decay of the differentiated Oseen kernel

rows.fidelity_note:
There is one finite real constant $C$ such that, for every $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\tau>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $|H_{ijk}(\tau,x)|\le C/(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^4$. Here $H_{ijk}=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho\,d\rho$, with the standard three-dimensional heat kernel $G_\rho$; it represents $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$. The constant is uniform in space, positive time and all three coordinate indices. The inequality is componentwise. A norm bound for the entire first derivative follows by summing finitely many components and changing the constant. The exponent $4$ is a fixed natural-number power, and $|x|+\sqrt\tau>0$ under the hypothesis. The paper's (3.9) allows every nonnegative integer derivative order $l$, with a constant depending on $l$. This theorem gives its first-derivative case only.

The formal kernel estimate is $C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}$ for all $\tau>0$ and all $x$, which implies the stated time-uniform $C|x|^{-4}$ estimate away from the origin.
rows.name: Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_holds
rows.plain: Fourth-power spatial decay of the differentiated Oseen kernel
rows.annotation: For $x\in Q_L$ and $x\prime\in B_{L/8}$, the distance to the translated source at $x\prime+Lj$ is at least $3L|j|_\infty/8$ for $j\ne0$. Consequently the sum of the noncentral heat responses is bounded by $CL^{-4}\|F\|_1$ and its gradient by $CL^{-5}\|F\|_1$, using (3.9) for derivatives of orders one and two. Taking the $L^6$ and gradient $L^2$ norms over the cell gives $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$ in each case. The linked `lerayKernelBound_holds` supplies the first-derivative bound; the second is also needed for (6.2).

ties.name: Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation
ties.plain: Correcting a periodic approximate flow on all time intervals

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X,E$ be real Banach spaces. For each integer $n\ge0$, let $G_n$ be a strongly continuous contraction heat semigroup and $K_n$ a continuous symmetric bilinear kernel satisfying $G_n(s)K_n(\tau)=K_n(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, with $\|K_n(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, where $C_K\ge0$ is independent of $n$. Fix $0<\ell\le1$, $0<\theta<1$, a real endpoint factor $c$, bounded linear $J:E\to X$, and continuous interval curves $a_n,r_n:[0,\ell]\to X$. Assume $\|a_n\|_\infty\le M$, $a_{n+1}(0)=c\,a_n(\ell)$, $a_n=G_n(\cdot)a_n(0)+\mathcal B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n$, and $\|r_n\|_\infty\le\theta^n\rho$. Here $\mathcal B_n(f,g)(s)=\int_0^sK_n(s-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

Suppose a bounded linear map $R$ takes each bounded interval sequence $g$ to $(e,z)$ satisfying $z_n-2\mathcal B_n(a_n,z_n)-G_n(\cdot)Je=g_0$ for $n=0$, and $z_n-2\mathcal B_n(a_n,z_n)-(c/\theta)G_n(\cdot)z_{n-1}(\ell)=g_n$ for $n\ge1$.

For a datum displacement $\xi\in X$, assume $64\|R\|^2C_K\ell^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$.

The formal statement asserts an $e$ and curves $z_n$ with $\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_\infty\le2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$, such that, on writing $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$, each $v_n$ satisfies $v_n(s)=G_n(s)v_n(0)+\mathcal B_n(v_n,v_n)(s)$ on the closed interval, with an integrable nonlinear term. Moreover $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(\ell)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The sequence norm is the supremum over the interval index and time, and the product norm is the maximum of its two factor norms. The positive hypotheses exclude zero denominators.

The formal statement is this implication, and it is proved.

Finite dimensionality of $E$ is not assumed. The separate bounds on the residual and datum displacement do not retain possible cancellation in the paper's combined forcing $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}$. The paper asserts removal of the particular cutoff residual and a physical solution on the torus. This conditional sequence assertion supplies exact matched mild pieces once its residual, inverse and smallness hypotheses hold. It does not itself verify those hypotheses for the cutoff or identify and join the final physical solution.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation
rows.plain: Correcting a periodic approximate flow on all time intervals
rows.annotation: The paper chooses $\kappa$ by the whole-space spectral argument. In the sequence construction let $\lambda=e^{-S/k}$ for $k$ subdivisions of a return, $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $t_n=T-\mu_n$. The selected weight $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ can be written $\theta=\lambda^\kappa$ with $0<\kappa<1/4$. The normalized velocity is $U_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u(t_n+\mu_ns)$, on $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. Writing $U_n=\bar U_n+\theta^n z_n$ with bounded $z_n$, endpoint matching forces $z_{n+1}(0)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)z_n(1-\lambda)$. This ratio is less than one. The physical error is bounded by $C\mu_n^{-1/4}\theta^n=CT^{-\kappa}\mu_n^{\kappa-1/4}$, which has the rate of (4.5) since $\lambda\mu_n\le T-t\le\mu_n$.

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal statement defines an existence assertion on the unit torus. There are a smooth field $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with period one in each coordinate and zero divergence, a real $T>0$, and a continuous mild curve $u$ on $[0,T)$ whose initial state is the Fourier representation of $u_0$, such that $\sup_{0\le t<T}\|u(t)\|=\infty$. The periodic state has coordinates $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,\widehat u(k)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$, with conjugate symmetry and $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$; its norm is the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm on the unit cell. The zero coefficient is allowed, so this state space does not impose zero mean. The initial-field map returns zero outside its admissible Fourier class; smooth periodic solenoidal data belong to that class. Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation for every $0\le t<T$, with convergent time integrals. The assertion imposes neither $T\le1$ nor either estimate in (2.6), gives no local comparison on $B_{1/16}$, and states unboundedness rather than a specified limit or rate at $T$. It contains no smooth velocity-pressure representative of the curve. This is the existence condition; a separate construction proves it from a profile.

The formal target retains a unit-periodic mild trajectory with unbounded $H^1$ norm, without the paper's explicit rescaling formula or quantitative bounds.

Hence the gradient norm gains $L^{1/2}$, and $L^{1/2}(1-L^2t)^{-1/4}=(T-t)^{-1/4}$ for $T=L^{-2}$. The region of exact agreement of the approximate field with the reference field shrinks from $B_{L/16}$ to $B_{1/16}$. `TorusBlowup` retains the unboundedness conclusion, not the quantitative rate or the local comparison.

citations.supports: For a nonzero smooth ordinary backward DSS solution in the stated integrability class, the local cubic integral grows without bound as the ball radius tends to infinity at any fixed time.
citations.title: The logarithmic lower bound for ordinary DSS

explanation.text: The factor $(T-t)^{-3/2}$ from cubing the velocity cancels the volume factor $(T-t)^{3/2}$. For a nonzero ordinary backward discretely self-similar profile with $R=I$, the Barker–Prange bound gives a logarithmic lower bound for the cubic integral in similarity variables. A slice in $L^2\cap L^6$ would lie in $L^3$, so each slice of the reference profile has infinite energy.

rows.annotation: The fields in $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ are solenoidal pointwise, not merely after projection. Finite linear combinations stay in this class, so a correction chosen in a finite-dimensional span of these fields changes neither compact support nor smoothness of the datum. Density of the class in $X$ is a separate result in Subsection 3.1.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.X
ties.plain: The homogeneous solenoidal space

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal space $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ consisting of classes $g$ such that $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The first condition represents a real velocity; the second represents zero divergence. The interpretation for a physical velocity $u$ is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, with the Fourier convention $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. Thus the norm on the formal space is $\|g\|_2$, corresponding to $\|\nabla u\|_2$. Elements are classes modulo equality almost everywhere, with no smoothness imposed. The denominator in the longitudinal projection is $|\xi|^2$; its reciprocal is assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which does not affect an $L^2$ class. The paper defines $X$ as divergence-free physical fields in $L^6$ with gradient in $L^2$. Identifying that description with this Fourier space requires the reconstruction and density results. This definition by itself does not assert the paper's completion theorem for all fields.

The formal space stores the weighted frequency field $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ in a closed real solenoidal subspace of $L^2$; its physical $L^6$ velocity is reconstructed separately.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.X
rows.plain: The homogeneous solenoidal space
rows.annotation: The Fourier coordinate used for $X$ is $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The conditions $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ enforce a real, divergence-free velocity, and the $L^2$ norm of $g$ measures the gradient. The identification with physical $L^6$ fields uses the reconstruction and density results, not the definition of the subspace alone.

rows.fidelity_note:
For the real Hilbert space $X$ of solenoidal frequency classes $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with conjugation symmetry, this defines a bounded real linear map $V:X\to L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$. Its defining requirement is $V(J\varphi)=[\varphi]$ for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, where $J\varphi$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$ and brackets denote an equivalence class modulo equality almost everywhere. The definition chooses a map with this property if one exists and assigns the zero map otherwise. A separate theorem proves that such a map exists, so the zero choice does not occur. For arbitrary $g$, the output is an $L^6$ class, and pointwise evaluations use a representative. Equality of reconstructed fields in subsequent statements is usually almost everywhere. Boundedness yields $\|Vg\|_6\le\|V\|\|g\|_X$; this definition does not assign a numerical Sobolev constant.

This map reconstructs the physical $L^6$ velocity from the weighted frequency state; it is one part of the realization of the paper’s physical-space definition.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.velocity
rows.plain: Reconstructing the physical velocity
rows.annotation: To recover the velocity from $g$, take compact smooth solenoidal approximants in the weighted Fourier norm. The Sobolev inequality makes their physical velocities Cauchy in $L^6$, so the limit defines a bounded real linear map $V:X\to L^6$. This is the map selected by `velocity`; its existence is proved in `velocity_holds`.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.embedNormLinear_holds
ties.plain: The frequency norm equals the L² gradient norm

rows.fidelity_note:
For a smooth divergence-free field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, assume $|f(y)|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df(y)\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$ for one finite constant $A$ and every $y$. Its representation $Jf$ is formed from the $L^2$ Fourier transforms of the derivatives by $\sum_j(-i\xi_j/|\xi|)\widehat{\partial_j f}$; this equals the expected weighted transform $2\pi|\xi|\hat f$ when Fourier differentiation is used. The formal statement proves $\|Jf\|_X^2=\int\sum_{j=1}^3|\partial_j f|^2$, and proves that $J$ respects sums, differences and real scalar multiples of fields in this decay class. The norm of $X$ is the $L^2$ norm of the represented frequency class. The multipliers involving division by $|\xi|$ are assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which is a null set. This proves the physical energy identity for the stated smooth decay class; the statement does not quantify over every physical $L^6$ field with a weak gradient in $L^2$.

The formal equality identifies the squared norm with the integral of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives for smooth solenoidal fields with prescribed velocity and derivative decay. The paper states the norm on all of $X$.

rows.annotation: The squared norm of an embedded field is $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_j|\partial_j u|^2\,dx$. ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds
ties.plain: Heat semigroup on the homogeneous solenoidal space

rows.fidelity_note:
On the real Hilbert space $X$ of $L^2$ classes $g$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere, let $G(t)$ be multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$. The formal statement proves $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$, and continuity of $t\mapsto G(t)g$ on $[0,\infty)$ for each $g\in X$. An element $g$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, so $\|g\|_X$ corresponds to $\|\nabla u\|_2$ and $G(t)$ represents the paper's heat flow. Continuity is strong continuity for each fixed input, including the endpoint $0$; no continuity in operator norm at $0$ is asserted. Negative parameters use the identity extension and are outside the forward semigroup law.

The identity at time zero is proved for the heat operator on $X$. The paper’s convention covers every displayed $L^p$ space; the raw Gaussian integral at zero has a different default value.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.bilinX
ties.plain: The bilinear Navier–Stokes operator

assessments.fidelity_note:
For each $\tau>0$, the formal definition chooses a bounded real bilinear map $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ satisfying $\langle K(\tau)(u,v),\psi\rangle_X=-\tfrac12\int[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]\cdot\Phi_\tau\psi$ for every $u,v,\psi\in X$. The space $X$ is represented by real solenoidal frequency classes $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ in $L^2$, and physical velocities lie in $L^6$. The test field $\Phi_\tau\psi$ has frequency transform $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}g_\psi$, so for smooth fields it represents $-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}\psi$. If $\tau\le0$, or if no bounded bilinear map with the displayed property exists, the definition assigns the zero map. The supplied existence theorem proves that such a map exists for every $\tau>0$. The value at $\tau=0$ is consequently a convention; when it occurs at the endpoint of a time integral it is a single null-time value. The positive-time estimate and symmetry are separate statements.

The formal operator on all of $X$ is specified through the symmetrized transport pairing. The paper defines it directly through projected transport.

The formal statement proves $K(\tau)(J\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12H_\tau[(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi]$, as an equality in $X$. Here $J\varphi$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$ and $H_\tau$ sends a physical $L^2$ forcing to its projected heat evolution in the weighted frequency representation. ties.name: Breakdown.Periodic.V
ties.plain: The periodic Fourier space

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The conjugate symmetry is the reality condition and $n\cdot a(n)=0$ is the divergence-free condition. At $n=0$ the latter gives no restriction, which is why nonzero constants are included. The space is a closed real subspace of $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and is complete. A nonzero constant has positive formal norm and zero gradient norm, so the mean-zero restriction is essential in (3.16). Equation (3.15) instead uses the homogeneous norm on mean-zero fields of arbitrary period $L$. The distinction matters: the zero Fourier mode contributes to the formal norm, and no variable spatial period is a parameter of an element of the formal space.

The formal periodic space uses the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm on the fixed unit torus and permits a nonzero mean.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.V
rows.plain: The periodic Fourier space
rows.annotation: To represent a unit-period $H^1$ velocity, `V` uses the sequence $a(k)=\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,\hat u(k)$ in $\ell^2$. The conditions $a(-k)=\overline{a(k)}$ and $k\cdot a(k)=0$ express reality and solenoidality. In particular at $k=0$ the first condition makes $a(0)$ real and the second is vacuous. The paper instead uses the mean-zero space with the homogeneous gradient norm.

No behavior at $b$ or outside $[a,b)$ is required. This definition concerns the unit torus with its inhomogeneous norm, whereas §3.6 works in mean-zero homogeneous spaces at arbitrary period.

The same Duhamel form is imposed on a curve in that larger periodic Fourier space; zero mean is not part of the condition.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

A separate theorem proves this statement from the spectral dichotomy.

The formal statement produces a finite-dimensional correction parameter space, a lift into any dense linear data class, and a bounded right inverse for the linear recurrence. It does not yet state this nonlinear stability conclusion or its constants.

ties.name: Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds
ties.plain: Density of compact solenoidal fields

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X=\{g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)},\ \xi\cdot g(\xi)=0\text{ a.e.}\}$, with its real $L^2$ Hilbert norm. For a smooth compactly supported divergence-free field $\varphi$, write $J\varphi$ for its frequency representation $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$. The formal statement proves that the real linear span of these $J\varphi$ is dense in $X$. It also proves density in the graph norm of the negative Laplacian: if $g,h\in X$ satisfy $h(\xi)=4\pi^2|\xi|^2g(\xi)$ almost everywhere, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is such a $\varphi$ with $\|J\varphi-g\|_X<\varepsilon$ and $\|J(-\Delta\varphi)-h\|_X<\varepsilon$. A separate formal statement shows that every element of the indicated span is itself represented by one compact smooth divergence-free field. Thus the first conclusion gives the density used in §3.1; the graph approximation is additional information.

The formal density result permits approximation of every element of $X$ to every positive tolerance by the span of compact smooth solenoidal fields; it also gives approximation in the graph norm of the Laplacian.
rows.name: Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds

rows.annotation: The compact support is a requirement on the approximating velocity, not on its weighted Fourier transform. Let $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\rm div}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $T_0>0$, and let $u$ be a continuous mild curve in the Fourier representation of $\dot H^1_{\rm div}$ on the closed interval $[0,T_0]$, with $u(0)$ representing $\varphi$. For $\mu>0$, assume strongly continuous dilations satisfying $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For every $f$ in a dense subset of $X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with these operators at all their defined real parameters. rows.fidelity_note:
The formal space $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ consisting of classes $g$ such that $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The first condition represents a real velocity; the second represents zero divergence. The interpretation for a physical velocity $u$ is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, with the Fourier convention $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. Thus the norm on the formal space is $\|g\|_2$, corresponding to $\|\nabla u\|_2$. Elements are classes modulo equality almost everywhere, with no smoothness imposed. The denominator in the longitudinal projection is $|\xi|^2$; its reciprocal is assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which does not affect an $L^2$ class. The paper defines $X$ as divergence-free physical fields in $L^6$ with gradient in $L^2$. Identifying that description with this Fourier space requires the reconstruction and density results. This definition by itself does not assert the paper's completion theorem for all fields.

The formal state is the weighted Fourier realization of the homogeneous norm. This definition does not assert either set of blow-up estimates or their identification for the constructed smooth curve.

rows.annotation: The divergence is taken in the second index: $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)_j=\sum_m\partial_m(v_j u_m)=(u\cdot\nabla)v_j+v_j\operatorname{div}u$. Thus the order of the factors is reversed relative to the advection notation. Symmetrization in (3.10) includes both orders.

rows.annotation: The paper's $L^{6/5}$ kernel estimate gives convergence in $L^6$. ties.name: Breakdown.MonodromyStatement
