rows.plain: Bounded Duhamel and heat maps on one time interval
rows.annotation: For `pieceOperator` the bound is $4C_KT^{1/4}$ on the bilinear integral map for $T\le1$. rows.annotation: The projected evolution of a fixed mean-zero source has coefficients $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\mathbb P_k\hat f(k)$. rows.plain: Fifteen groups of cell-system hypotheses
rows.annotation: The cell conditions specify a single set of represented fields and compatible local quadratic forms. In particular the local unknowns used to prove coercivity are measurements of arbitrary perturbations, not a restriction of the perturbation to the splines. The join and pressure conditions allow the local inequalities to be summed for that same global field. rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive
rows.plain: Coercive estimate for the reference linearized equation
rows.annotation: Appendix B proves the inverse estimate by combining two inequalities. In (B.20) and (B.21) the integrals of the mode density and the stretching term, as well as the pairing of the unknown force with $\mathsf Mv$, disappear when the inequalities are combined. Lemma B.2 then has the scalar form $P^2\le c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}P+Q^2$, with $P^2$ containing $\frac3{50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2$ and $Q^2=\frac3{50}[F]^2+1000|\ell(v)|^2$. Bounding the positive root by $c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+Q$ and using $\sqrt{3/50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le P$ gives (7.18). The cell computations thus bound an inverse on the full domain, not the smallest singular value of the discretization alone.

rows.fidelity_note: The change-of-profile estimate is an assumption for every admissible invariant perturbation.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gap_transfer
rows.plain: Linearized convection gap between the approximate and reference profiles
rows.annotation: Lemma B.9 estimates the change $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$ in the convection operator by $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. Applying the reference estimate to $F-G$ costs at most $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ in addition to the cost of $F$. Hence (7.21) makes the extra cost absorbable into the left side of (7.52).

rows.fidelity_note: The quadratic adjoint bound is assumed for every admissible invariant perturbation.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_quadratic
rows.plain: The quadratic adjoint estimate
rows.annotation: Lemma B.10 permits either a slice $L^3$ or a slice $L^2$ bound on $\psi_j$. In the first case estimate the velocity factors in $L^6$ and $L^2$; in the second use $L^\infty$ and $L^2$. Both products are bounded by constants times $|v(\theta)|_w^2$, which can be integrated over one period. This is why the adjoint error is quadratic in $\|v\|_w$, rather than requiring a separate bound on the maximum gradient in time.

rows.fidelity_note: The linear adjoint bound is assumed for every admissible perturbation and every square-integrable right-side representative.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_defect
rows.plain: The linear adjoint error
rows.annotation: The adjoint defect is an estimate for a linear functional of $v$, not an $L^2$ norm of an adjoint residual. Lemma B.11 uses Hardy's inequality to bound $|\int v\cdot R|$ by $2\||y|R\|_{\mathcal H}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ for the unstructured part of a defect field $R$; its azimuthal decomposition improves the estimate for nonzero wave numbers. This is suited to the homogeneous space, in which $v$ itself need not belong to $\mathcal H$. Lemma B.12 then incorporates the constraint fields and the remaining terms of the adjoint identity.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal certificate assumes the reference form bound and a separate transfer bound; their sum gives the approximate-profile bound (7.22).
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frozen_form
rows.plain: Lower bound for the spatial form at the reference profile
rows.annotation: The transfer of the frozen form is a second use of the same convection difference. If $G(u)=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})u$ at a phase, the change in the form is $-\langle G(u),\Delta u\rangle_{L^2}$. Lemma B.9 controls this pairing from below; its contribution adds to the reference lower-bound constant rather than being absorbed as in (7.52). This gives the constant $c_3$ for the energy-growth estimate.

The complete formal condition includes these two comparisons and also the row-sum residual test, symmetry, positive weights and pivot lower bounds. At one node, let $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$, with the sum over its children, and let $V_\xi$ be the matrix passed to its parent. Given pivots $\mathcal U_\xi$ and columns $Y_\xi$, the condition supplies symmetric $H,K$, symmetric entrywise nonnegative $H',K'$, positive weights $w_j$, real $p_j,m_j$, and a rectangular real matrix $Y'$. For every real $x$ it requires $\langle Hx,x\rangle\le\langle Ax,x\rangle+\langle H'|x|,|x|\rangle$ and $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle\le\langle Kx,x\rangle-\sum_{j\notin\mathcal U_\xi}m_jx_j^2+\langle K'|x|,|x|\rangle$. For each row, $w_i\sum_j(|B_{ij}|+H'_{ij}+K'_{ij})/w_j\le m_i$, where $B=H-\operatorname{diag}_{\mathcal U_\xi}(p)-Y'Y'^T+Y_\xi Y_\xi^T-K$ and the diagonal is zero off the pivots. On each pivot $\underline p_{\xi,j}\le p_j-m_j$. Here $|x|$ means componentwise absolute value. All spaces are finite-dimensional and the forms are real. The positive weights exclude zero denominators. These are assumptions on the supplied node matrices and bounds; they perform no numerical verification themselves.

The formal lower bound retains the root’s passed quadratic form. Dropping it under the nonnegativity hypothesis yields the displayed inequality. For finite sets of determined and free real coordinates and a finite collection of nodes, suppose the root has no parent and every other node has exactly one assigned parent. At each node assume, for every real $x$, $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_\xi}\underline p_{\xi,j}x_j^2-|Y_\xi^Tx|^2\le\langle N_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{\xi'}\langle V_{\xi'}x,x\rangle$, where $\xi'$ ranges over children. Then $\langle Nx,x\rangle\ge\langle V_{\rm root}x,x\rangle+\sum_\xi\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_\xi}\underline p_{\xi,j}x_j^2-\sum_\xi|Y_\xi^Tx|^2$ for every real $x$, with $N=\sum_\xi N_\xi$. Each non-root passed matrix occurs once on each side in the sum. No separate connectedness or acyclicity hypothesis is required for this cancellation identity. The theorem retains the root term; the paper's (B.41) follows when that term is nonnegative. It assumes neither positive pivot lower bounds nor coverage of all coordinates, and thus does not alone imply strict positivity on the common column kernel.

rows.plain: The weak azimuthal Hardy bound
rows.annotation: Averaging a smooth approximant against $e^{-ik\phi'}$ preserves compact support in a ball and contracts the gradient norm. In the paper this gives approximants to a function of fixed wave number. rows.plain: Total azimuthal energy is bounded by the gradient energy
rows.annotation: Orthogonality is with respect to the gradient inner product, so finite $L^2$ mass of the velocity is not required. In Lean `gradientModeTotal` is the spatial Bessel inequality, for the angular projections of the derivative matrix on a slice. It bounds the sum of all angular gradient contributions by the gradient energy; time integration is carried out separately.

rows.name: Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.timeModeSum
rows.plain: Orthogonality of the temporal harmonics
rows.annotation: The paper projects the test in time as well as angle. Lean uses temporal orthogonality on the given field instead: for a fixed component and angular number, put $B_k(\theta,y)=\sum_{k'}e^{2\pi ik'\theta}g_{k',k}(y)$. Integrating $\||y|B_k(\theta)\|_2^2$ over one period gives the sum of $\||y|g_{k',k}\|_2^2$ by distinctness of the time integers. This is the estimate in `timeModeSum`; it requires no time derivative of the test.

rows.name: Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.modePairing
rows.plain: Pairing with one azimuthal mode
rows.annotation: In the paper the two averages select $u_{k',k}$; only this projection pairs with $e^{2\pi ik'\theta}g$. The linked `modePairing` works at a fixed time: for a scalar amplitude $B$ of angular number $k$, rotation gives the pairing with $P_ku$, which is bounded by $\|P_ku/|y|\|_2\||y|B\|_2$. rows.annotation: The paper applies Cauchy–Schwarz to the gradient norms of the double projections and the weighted norms of their partners. In Lean, at time $\theta$, let $E(\theta)$ be the gradient energy and $A(\theta)$ the weighted sum of squared norms of the grouped angular amplitudes. rows.annotation: The complex components are a redundant representation of a real vector. The sum of $(v_1+i v_2)\overline{(R_1+iR_2)}$ and $(v_1-i v_2)\overline{(R_1-iR_2)}$ is $2(v_1R_1+v_2R_2)$. Half of this sum, plus $v_3R_3$, is the original pairing. No imaginary part remains.

rows.annotation: The half weights on the two horizontal complex components are needed on both sides of Cauchy–Schwarz: their weighted gradient energies sum to the horizontal gradient energy of $v$. ties.name: Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField
ties.plain: Periodicity, decay and weak derivatives of adjoint fields

rows.fidelity_note: The analytic condition allows any decay exponent $\gamma >5/2$ and only requires second-derivative decay of order $\gamma$; the printed representation gives the sharper orders 3, 4 and 5.
rows.name: Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField
rows.plain: Periodicity, decay and weak derivatives of adjoint fields
rows.annotation: For the adjoint transport terms, $\psi_j$, $\partial_\theta\psi_j$ and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ decay at the same rate. To pair them with an $L^6$ velocity one needs exponent $h>5/2$ so that they are in $L^{6/5}$. The represented fields have $h\ge3$. The general formal `IsAdjointField` uses an exponent $\gamma>5/2$ and weak spatial second derivatives; its bound for the latter only uses exponent $\gamma$, not $\gamma+2$.

rows.name: Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData
rows.plain: Decay and weak derivatives of the adjoint potentials
rows.annotation: The auxiliary fields are a way of representing a functional of the perturbation in norms already present in (7.14). A term $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ can be paired with $\Delta v$ by moving two derivatives, whereas $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ can be paired through the gradients by moving one. Thus a potential of size $O(|y|^{-1})$ is allowed for $\mathsf U_j$, even though it need not have finite $L^2$ norm. The remaining defect is measured by B.11.

rows.name: Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ballPairing
rows.plain: Period pairing inside the matching ball
rows.annotation: Solenoidality removes a gradient from a pairing on all of space under the indicated integrability hypotheses. Thus the pressure and kinetic-energy gradients in (B.57) are retained in (B.58). Lean integrates on the closed ball; the sphere has measure zero.

rows.name: Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.logPhaseIsRadial
rows.plain: Regularity of the logarithmic phase
rows.annotation: For $f(\rho)=A\log(1+\rho/r_c^2)$ one has $\rho^j|f^{(j)}(\rho)|=|A|(j-1)!(\rho/(r_c^2+\rho))^j$ for $j=1,2,3$. These are bounded by $|A|(j-1)!$ since $r_c>0$. Thus the phase grows logarithmically but meets exactly the derivative conditions of B.1.

rows.name: Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase
rows.plain: The harmonic with radial phase
rows.annotation: At fixed $x\ne0$, the substitution (1.4) gives exactly $\log((T-t)+|x|^2/r_c^2)-\log T$ in the square brackets. The cancellation of the two $\log(T-t)$ terms explains the phase choice. A pointwise Eulerian limit still requires the leading meridian amplitudes to have the asymptotics stated below; the bound (7.38) for the corrected field is not such an expansion.

ties.plain: The similarity momentum residual

assessments.fidelity_note: The formal expression uses advection, $-\Delta W$ and pressure $q$, and does not impose either equation. Smoothness, solenoidality and $H=q+|W|^2/2$ identify it with the printed residual.

rows.name: Breakdown.SimilarityResidual
rows.plain: The similarity momentum residual
rows.annotation: For a solenoidal smooth field, $-\Delta W=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W$. Also $(W\cdot\nabla)W=(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W+\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Substituting both identities into (1.2) gives the curl formulation, with the kinetic-energy gradient absorbed into $H$. `SimilarityResidual` uses the original advection and diffusion form.

assessments.fidelity_note: For smooth divergence-free $W$ the formal identity replaces the double curl by $-\Delta W$; it asserts neither the pressure equation nor vanishing of the residual.

rows.name: Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityProof.negSsp_curl_curl
rows.plain: The double-curl identity
rows.annotation: For any smooth vector field, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W=\nabla\operatorname{div}W-\Delta W$. In (C.1) the second displayed equation sets the first term on the right to zero. The linked lemma is the solenoidal specialization of this identity; it explains why the diffusion term in the residual of (C.1) is the positive double curl.

ties.name: Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Internal.RemainderAnnihilates.cross_identity
ties.plain: Subtracting the curl cross term transposes the matrix

rows.fidelity_note: The matrix identity gives the advection/curl-cross difference; identifying it with the kinetic-energy gradient also uses the chain rule for a differentiable field.
rows.name: Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Internal.RemainderAnnihilates.cross_identity
rows.plain: Subtracting the curl cross term transposes the matrix
rows.annotation: At a fixed point set $M=DW(y)$ and $x=W(y)$. The linked identity, tested against every vector $\psi$, is $Mx-(\operatorname{curl}W)\times x=M^Tx$. The chain rule gives $M^Tx=\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Hence the pressure in the curl formulation is $q+|W|^2/2$, with the plus sign.

ties.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l2
ties.plain: The residual norm bound

rows.fidelity_note: The residual norm bound uses one threshold for every certified parameter. This is the uniform verification input, separate from the paper’s exploratory fitting diagnostic.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l2
rows.note: The residual norm bound uses one threshold for every certified parameter. This is the uniform verification input, separate from the paper’s exploratory fitting diagnostic.
rows.plain: The residual norm bound
rows.annotation: The norm is that of a selected residual representative on the whole period and all of space. If one adds a gradient to that representative the projected equation is unchanged, but the norm entering the inverse budget need not be unchanged. `defect_l2` bounds this selected field by $\delta(\alpha)$ at each parameter. The further bound by $\delta_{\max}$ is used when one common estimate is needed for the whole family.

rows.fidelity_note: The sampled residual row bounds also use one budget uniformly over the certified parameter set.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_rows
rows.note: The sampled residual row bounds also use one budget uniformly over the certified parameter set.
rows.plain: Weighted row seminorm bound for the approximate residual
rows.annotation: The row bound controls the vector of weighted residual pairings, not the individual coefficients of the auxiliary force. It is possible to have $[F]=0$ and $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}>0$ when the residual is orthogonal to every row. The separate inequality $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\le\delta_0(\alpha)$ preserves that information in (7.24); the quadratic trial, for which no comparable directional information is given, uses the general bound (7.17).

rows.plain: The linearized residual identity
rows.annotation: The differential expression in (C.2) is the linearization at the current profile. The formal strong right-hand side also allows the actuator forcing and the gradient of pressure: its diffusion term is minus the Hessian trace, using solenoidality to replace $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v$ by $-\Delta v$. In Appendix C the expression is tested in a finite space to find an approximate field; in Appendix B its cellwise pairings are estimated for arbitrary perturbations of the reference field.

rows.name: Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.affineField

rows.plain: Affine profile inside the ball
rows.annotation: At a fixed phase the represented field is the center plus $\sum_i\alpha_i$ times the corresponding tangent fields, evaluated at the same phase. In the region where $f_*=0$, the phase correction in (B.9) disappears and gives this affine representation. `affineField` defines the latter expression; its agreement with the phase-dependent field on the ball needs a separate identity.

ties.name: Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq
ties.plain: Frequency in a rotating frame

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition calculates the shifted frequency from the time harmonic, angular harmonic and frame rotation rate.
rows.name: Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq
rows.note: The formal definition calculates the shifted frequency from the time harmonic, angular harmonic and frame rotation rate.
rows.plain: Frequency in a rotating frame
rows.annotation: For $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$, the two frequencies at the trial period are $2\pi j/S(\alpha)\pm2\pi\iota_1/\bar S$. The larger absolute value is $2\pi(|j|/S(\alpha)+|\iota_1|/\bar S)$, attained by choosing a sign for which the summands agree in sign. The same choice works for every positive trial period. Thus if $S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$, this modulus is at least $\min(1,\bar S/S_{\max})$ times the central maximum. This explains how a lower bound can persist under period changes; admissibility still has to be checked on the actual selected sets.
